mentions.note: Supposedly named after the average volume of a man's ejaculation.

term: a magpie brought it on its tail
translation: a magpie brought it on its tail

mentions.note: A Russian counterpart of [[a little bird told me]] that features a magpie instead of a little bird.

term: a shrimp that falls asleep gets carried away by the current
translation: a shrimp that falls asleep gets carried away by the current

mentions.note: Similar to 'you snooze, you lose'.
A Latin suffix English happily adds to Germanic stems (watchable, winnable, knowable), making hybrids alongside Romance words like visible and portable.

From Latin altare, a Christian-era borrowing; it's thought to come from [[adolere]], 'to burn', rather than altus, 'high', because offerings were burned there.

Replaced the older [[apples and oysters]] in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, first for false equivalences between similar-looking things, though now used for very different things.

Cockney rhyming slang for stairs, which Rob thinks of before [[apples and oranges]].
Originally a sandy place, since Roman amphitheatres were strewn with sand to soak up blood; the exact root is unknown and may be Etruscan.
Built up through Johnny Appleseed, early American cookbooks, pie as a symbol of prosperity, and WWII soldiers fighting for 'mom and apple pie'.
The Croatian way to describe heavy rain; Rob would rather take his chances with the cats.
The saying that one rotten apple spoils the rest appears in a 1528 Reformation pamphlet and, earlier, a 1340 Kentish moral treatise.
1920s slang for nonsense, named after banana-scented amyl acetate, an artificial chemical; Rube Goldberg popularized it in his comic strips.
From hunting: beating bushes to scare birds out rather than going straight for them.

term: better a bird in the hand than a hundred flying
original: más vale pájaro en mano que ciento volando
translation: better a bird in the hand than a hundred flying

mentions.note: A slight variation on the English [[a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush]].

term: between a dog and a wolf
translation: between a dog and a wolf

19th-century slang for something desirable or sure; it stuck to New York after sportswriter John J. Fitz Gerald used it in 1921 for the city's rich racetracks.
William Barnes's Germanic alternative to ornithology, alongside [[starlore]].

translation: birds hear words spoken by day and mice hear words spoken by night

Named after a Boris Karloff horror film showing nearby, in the hope that people would pay to see them the way they paid for horror films.

A Colombian Spanish expression for daydreaming.
A 1600s term for harmful spirits, hallucinations and mental anguish that Jefferson and Byron used to mean sadness; later shortened to [[blues|the blues]].
From [[blue devils]]. Its first printed musical use is in Charlotte Forten Grimké's diary; the genre was named after song titles like Memphis Blues.
1970s slang for the television, whose watchers became 'boob tubers', the likely pun behind [[couch potato]]; in Britain it's also a 1990s garment.
Real book-eating pests such as silverfish, book lice or beetle larvae are called bookworms; 'worm' for vermin needn't mean an actual worm.

Covered in an earlier idiom episode; most likely wishes someone bad luck so they get good luck, and the hosts reject the 'being in a cast' explanation.
A Hungarian good-luck wish that closely resembles the English [[break a leg]].
A German good-luck wish that is very close to the English [[break a leg]].

term: broken Irish is better than clever English
translation: broken Irish is better than clever English

mentions.note: Encourages people to speak Irish even badly; it rhymes in Irish and carries a lot of historical baggage.

Taken from Latin on the continent, originally in a battle sense; related to German Kampf and to the later French borrowings [[campaign]] and [[champion]].
Stage name of Brian Cassar, borrowed from the Ballad of Casey Jones.
From Latin castellum, a fort or stronghold, which entered late Old English through biblical usage; it was later borrowed again from French as château.
Jess finds it somewhat derogatory, a taunt aimed at someone who can't or won't speak.
[[verlan|Verlan]] form of français.
Like [[wine]], a Latin word taken from the Romans by Germanic speakers before English existed.
From the art episode; meaning 'bright dark', it shares its dark element with [[obscure]].
The usual explanation is that someone wanting a fight would put a wood chip on their shoulder and dare others to knock it off.
[[verlan|Verlan]] form of merci.
Formerly Big Fat Noises and Starfish; named after Philip Horky's 1997 poetry collection Child's Reflections, Cold Play.
To carry something with you along a road, from [[via]].
Latin for 'body', whose plural is corpora, not corpi.
The Spanish version of [[cost an arm and a leg]]; Jess thinks it's the mildest price, since you have two kidneys.

term: cost an arm and a leg

mentions.note: Losing an arm and a leg would be a very heavy price to pay, so the phrase means something is very expensive.

term: cost the eyes of your head
translation: to cost the eyes in your head

mentions.note: The French version of [[cost an arm and a leg]]; Rob points out that you lose both eyes.
Supposedly coined in 1976 by Tom Iacino, probably a pun on [[boob tube]] watchers as 'tubers'; other theories involve slouching or being vegetative.
A theological counterpart to [[agenda]]: things to be believed alongside things to be done.
Cheke's substitute for crucified, which Jess says sounds like a euphemism.
A Bosnian equivalent of [[raining cats and dogs]].
Slang for coffee first recorded in the 1930s, probably from [[jamoke]]; the Josephus Daniels navy alcohol ban theory lacks evidence, and the average-Joe idea is also unlikely.
'Not my cup of tea' dates to 1908 and was popularized by Punch in the 1930s; it rests on everyone liking their tea differently.
Originally Darlin', after a Beach Boys single; renamed after a Melody Maker review called their music "a daft punky thrash."
A British political term for a shocking distraction, as if a dead cat were put on the table so no one discusses the real issue.
Means having nothing going on, being bored or wasting time; the source of the band name [[Die Toten Hosen]].
Originally Deaf Leopard, coined in a school art lesson and respelled for fun; the band liked that it echoed [[Led Zeppelin]].
To stray away from the course, from [[via]].
Being devious or deviant means straying from the moral path, from [[via]].
Originally 'lasting one day', from [[dies]]; a doublet of [[journal]], covered in a previous episode.
German band whose name means the doctors.
German band whose name comes from the idiom [[dead trousers]], meaning to have nothing going on.
Latin prefix meaning not, away or broadly, as in distribute; French words beginning de- or des- carry the same prefix after it passed through French.
From medieval Latin dies mali, the two unlucky days each month, also called [[Egyptian days]]; first used in 'in the dismal', then the tautological 'dismal day'.
Cockney rhyming slang for the telephone, given as an example of rhyming slang in everyday British speech.

term: don't call anything splendid until you've seen Nikko
original: Nikkō o mizu shite kekkō to iu nakare
translation: don't call anything splendid until you've seen Nikko

mentions.note: Praises Nikko's shrine complex and puns on 'Nikko' and 'kekko' (splendid); the hosts compare it to Goethe's [[see Naples and die]].

term: don't scald your lips on another man's porridge
translation: don't scald your lips on another man's porridge

mentions.note: Advice to stay out of other people's business and problems.
Another name for the dies mali behind [[dismal]], supposedly calculated by ancient Egyptian scholars or linked to the story of the plagues.
One of the words Jess used with fifth graders to teach a Latin root meaning 'to talk', along with [[loquacious]] and [[soliloquy]].
Someone sent somewhere to represent someone else; from [[via]] and related to [[invoice]].
A reassuring saying that even experts sometimes make mistakes.
In Quebec French, like 'fasten your seat belt'; a toque here is a winter hat, though the word can also mean a chef's hat.
Roman calendar lists of official and religious events and of dies fasti, days allowed for business; Jess enjoys that the source is 'the fasti of Furius'.
A fan praised their music as fettes Brot, slang for really good hash, since fett meant great and Brot meant hash.

term: flies don't enter a closed mouth
original: en boca cerrada no entran moscas
translation: flies don't enter a closed mouth

mentions.note: Advice to keep your mouth shut to stay out of trouble.
Means hardly anyone showed up, roughly like 'one man and his dog'.
1800s stable slang for horses fed on beans before a race or hunt and in fit condition; it once also meant arrogant or purse-proud.
Dates to at least the early 1900s and was adapted into [[go bananas]].
Adapted from [[go ape]] by linking monkeys with bananas, with 'bananas' alone recorded from the 1920s, though wild monkeys rarely eat bananas.
Describes someone who trails around after someone else, the way poop dangles behind a goldfish.
Grand ('big') plus the root meaning 'to talk', so literally 'big talking'; William Barnes proposed [[high-talking]] in its place.
Literally means [[pomegranate]], which grenades resemble, and when they explode bits burst out like pomegranate seeds.
A genre name given by people who disliked the music and then adopted by it, like [[punk]].
Originally just a person's name, now used for any person, another example of everyman names.

term: he keeps a hedgehog in his pocket
translation: he keeps a hedgehog in his pocket

mentions.note: Describes a stingy person: reaching into a pocket with a hedgehog in it would hurt, so they avoid paying.
William Barnes's Germanic replacement for [[grandiloquent]].
Industry term for bluegrass-style music marketed to white audiences, the counterpart of [[race records]]; it developed into country music.

term: how do you like them apples

mentions.note: Found in 1895 in Texas's Bryan Daily Eagle, boasting about cotton receipts; the WWI toffee-apple mortar story is too late to be the source.
A 19th-century phrase, probably a pun on [[umbles|umble pie]], a lowly dish of deer entrails given to servants.
Sir John Cheke's native replacement for centurion in his Gospel of Matthew, written to avoid excessive borrowings in the [[inkhorn]] spirit.
Means hunger makes food taste better; Jess feels it carries historical baggage but is meant optimistically.
A Taylor Swift lyric that became a meme; Jess picked it up without realising it came from the song.
Im- 'not', per 'through' and [[via]] 'road': something with no way through, and so resistant to attack.
Name of the backlash against classical borrowings during the Renaissance; perhaps because long Latinate words meant dipping your quill into an inkhorn again and again.
An 18th-century non-hybrid alternative to [[interplanetary]], with mundane meaning worldly.
A hybrid of Latin inter and Greek planet; avoiding such hybrids produced [[intermundane]].
The Italian equivalent of [[break a leg]], which has a set reply, [[may the wolf die]].
Related to [[envoy]]: a request for payment to be sent along. There's no voice in it, but there is a road ([[via]]).
Rob's wife once said it in English; heavy rain looks like dangling strings, a French equivalent of [[raining cats and dogs]].
Late-19th-century American slang for coffee, a blend of [[java]] and [[mocha]], and the likely source of [[cup of joe]].
In Latin a doorkeeper or porter, related to [[Janus]], the two-faced god of doorways; it later meant a school usher, then a caretaker by the 1700s.
Named after [[Janus]], the god related to [[janitor]].
A greeting that is bonjour reversed in [[verlan]].
The word diurnal squeezed through French; a doublet of [[diary]].
African-American term for an informal venue with music, dancing and gambling; juke probably comes from a Gullah word meaning rowdy or disorderly.
Named after the [[juke joint]].
American, first recorded in 1891, so not from OED editor C. T. Onions; the Cockney rhyming slang onion rings = things is possible but puzzling.
Means power station, chosen because the band was into industry.

From the remark that the supergroup would [[go down like a lead balloon]]; the spelling was changed so people wouldn't read it as the verb lead.

term: let the cat out of the bag

mentions.note: Covered in an earlier episode: it isn't about the cat-o'-nine-tails but about buying a [[pig in a poke]] and finding a worthless cat inside.
The Spanish equivalent of [[bookworm]].

term: lie back and think of England

mentions.note: A British phrase about letting your mind wander during sex, which implies bad sex; Jess says it isn't used in America.

mentions.note: Means raising an awkward subject everyone avoids, like addressing the elephant in the room; almost the inverse of the British [[dead cat]].

The Macarena singers; the name means those from the river.
The band behind La Bamba; the name means the wolves.
Deliberately misspelled but still pronounced Leonard Skinner, after a gym teacher at the band's school.

Latin for 'hand', whose plural is also manus, not mani.

translation: mention a wolf and the wolf is there

mentions.note: A listener-submitted Lithuanian equivalent of [[speak of the devil]].

French for a tip, meaning money for a drink, like [[Trinkgeld]] and [[propina]].

Spanish for a tip, which goes back to a term for buying or having a drink, like [[Trinkgeld]] and [[pourboire]].

A word meaning horrible or inferior, applied to the music by its critics and then embraced by the musicians themselves.

translation: it's raining like a pissing cow

translation: raise crows and they will peck out your eyes

mentions.note: Jess reads it as bad parenting choices coming back to haunt you, or more generally like 'you reap what you sow'.
Named after their own song about the air-show crash at the US base Ramstein; the extra M comes from a misspelling on their equipment.
The Spanish [[spill the beans]]; the hosts aren't sure what the secret cake refers to.

From Cleopatra's line in Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra: being green and cold like lettuce means naive, like unripe fruit.

From Latin scrinium, a chest; it came to mean a chest holding a saint's relic, then a venerated place itself.

term: slide in on a shrimp sandwich
translation: slide in on a shrimp sandwich

Sleepwalking; the word Rob was reaching for after [[obambulation]].
Sleep-talking; the pupils worked it out from [[insomnia]] and the talk root in [[grandiloquent]].
From Aesop's fox, who calls the grapes he can't reach sour; it became an idiom around the 1760s, and Mark Twain revived it in Tom Sawyer.

Short for 'speak of the devil and he will appear'; many languages have variants.

William Barnes's Germanic alternative to astronomy.

Named after a dildo in William S. Burroughs's Naked Lunch, because the band loved Beat Generation literature.

A slightly newer version of [[tempest in a teapot]], with the same idea.
From Latin strata, as in [[via]] strata, a straight road, so saying street is essentially saying 'straight'.
The Belgian singer's name is [[maestro]] with its syllables swapped, in [[verlan]].

Goes back to the early 1800s, a little earlier than [[storm in a teacup]].
Latin 'to hold', found in [[maintain]], abstain, entertain, obtain and detain.
A pun on beetles and beat, partly inspired by Buddy Holly's Crickets; coined by John Lennon and Stuart Sutcliffe.

term: the cat climbed onto the roof
translation: the cat climbed onto the roof

mentions.note: Means a person or plan seems doomed; it comes from a joke about a servant told to break bad news gradually.

term: the devil knows more for being old than for being the devil
original: más sabe el diablo por viejo que por diablo
translation: the devil knows more because he is old than because he is the devil

Named after Aldous Huxley's mescaline essay The Doors of Perception, whose title quotes William Blake.
Originally the Ravens; the name was probably a gimmick hinting at kinkiness, meant to be subversive and to get publicity.

A Colombian Spanish expression for daydreaming, with a double entendre on rooster testicles.

translation: thinking about the immortality of the crab

term: thinking about the immortality of the maybug
translation: thinking about the immortality of the maybug

mentions.note: Used in Czech and Slovak for daydreaming; a variant of [[thinking about the immortality of the crab]].

term: thinking about the immortality of the mosquito
translation: thinking about the immortality of the mosquito

mentions.note: The Peruvian Spanish variant of [[thinking about the immortality of the crab]].

term: to end up like Zabłocki with his soap
translation: to end up like Zabłocki did with his soap

mentions.note: Used when a clever profit scheme loses money; it comes from a tale of a man who smuggled soap underwater and watched it dissolve.

term: to feel it while wearing clogs

term: to have one's tongue in one's pocket
original: avoir la langue dans sa poche
translation: to have one's tongue in one's pocket

mentions.note: A Québécois expression for a shy or silent person, gentler than the taunting [[cat's got your tongue]].

term: to have shat in the blue cupboard
translation: to have shat in the blue cupboard
